Homer
HOH-mer
n. (Hebrew)
Hebrew chōmer, “a heap, large quantity,” from chāmar (to heap up); the largest Hebrew dry measure, equal to ten ephahs (approximately 6.5 bushels / 220 liters). Not to be confused with the Greek poet Homer.

📖 Biblical Definition

The homer (Hebrew chōmer, “a heap”) is the largest dry measure in the Hebrew system—ten ephahs, approximately 6.5 bushels or 220 liters of grain. The word appears across the OT in contexts of substantial agricultural reckoning, prophetic measurement, and the divinely-prescribed sacrificial offerings. Several major uses anchor the doctrine. First, the quail-providence in the wilderness: Numbers 11:32 records that, when the LORD answered the people’s craving for flesh by sending quails, he that gathered least gathered ten homers: and they spread them all abroad for themselves round about the camp. Even the least-energetic gatherer collected ten homers of quail—an immense quantity, illustrating the overwhelming abundance of the provision that nonetheless was followed by judgment (the plague at Kibroth-hattaavah for the people’s lusting). Second, the Levitical agricultural standards. Leviticus 27:16 prescribes the valuation of a field according to its seed: an homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver. The homer is the standard measuring-unit for agricultural reckoning of crops, land, and tribute. Third, the prophetic messages. Hosea 3:2 records the prophet’s purchase of his adulterous wife Gomer for fifteen pieces of silver, an homer of barley, and a half-homer of barley—a substantial price reflecting the seriousness of the redemption-figure. Isaiah 5:10 prophesies coming judgment in agricultural terms: yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah—the catastrophic crop-failure of judgment, where the seed sown is ten times what is harvested. Ezekiel 45:11, 14 prescribe the measurement-standards for the prophetic temple vision, with the homer as the standard. Fourth, the symbolic-prophetic. Hosea 7:8: Ephraim is a cake not turned; the imagery is bread-related, the unit-context grain-measurement, the substance the prophetic indictment of Israel’s incomplete-conversion (a cake baked on one side, raw on the other—externally religious, internally unrepentant). The homer therefore serves several biblical-narrative-and-prophetic functions: the large standard unit for agricultural reckoning, the measuring-figure for divine provision-or-judgment, the prophetic standard for crop-yield warnings, and the larger context for various symbolic uses. As with the other biblical weights and measures, the homer is no mere agricultural curiosity but the standardized measurement-unit on which the LORD’s precise prescriptions for sacrifice, tribute, and just commerce all depend.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Hebrew term.) HOMER: the largest Hebrew dry measure, equal to ten ephahs (approximately 6.5 bushels); the standard unit for substantial agricultural reckoning, prophetic crop-warnings (Isa 5:10), and the divinely-prescribed sacrificial-and-tribute standards.

HOMER, n. — (Hebrew dry-measure.) The largest dry-measure in the Hebrew system, equal to ten ephahs, approximately 6.5 bushels or 220 liters. Used across the OT for substantial agricultural reckoning (Lev 27:16), prophetic crop-warnings (Isa 5:10), and standardized measurement (Ezek 45:11, 14).

EPHAH, n. — A Hebrew dry-measure, approximately 22 liters; one-tenth of a homer.

📖 Key Scripture

Leviticus 27:16 — "And if a man shall sanctify unto the LORD some part of a field of his possession, then thy estimation shall be according to the seed thereof: an homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver."

Numbers 11:32 — "And the people stood up all that day, and all that night, and all the next day, and they gathered the quails: he that gathered least gathered ten homers: and they spread them all abroad for themselves round about the camp."

Isaiah 5:10 — "Yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah."

Hosea 3:2 — "So I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The homer as a biblical unit is corrupted in modern reading chiefly by being treated as quaint agricultural detail without operative theological substance—missing the structural use of the homer across the prophetic, sacrificial, and narrative literature as the standardized measurement-unit on which God’s precise prescriptions for sacrifice, tribute, and prophetic warning depend.

expand to see more

Modern readers tend to convert biblical weights and measures into approximate modern equivalents and skip the precision the OT writers preserved. The homer is one of many such units (ephah, bath, hin, log, seah, cab, omer, etc.) that contemporary preaching tends to treat as quaint agricultural curiosity without operative significance. The biblical writers used these units with deliberate precision: when Isaiah 5:10 says the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah, the prophetic-judgment severity depends on the reader knowing that an ephah is one-tenth of a homer, so the announcement is of a ten-to-one crop failure—catastrophic agricultural collapse as covenant judgment. When Leviticus 27:16 sets the valuation at fifty shekels for a homer of barley seed, the actual price-equivalent of a substantial agricultural transaction is being specified with precision. When Numbers 11:32 records that he that gathered least gathered ten homers of quail, the overwhelming abundance of the provision is being conveyed in concrete units. The recovery is the recovery of the precision, with the modern reader paying attention to the standardized units the OT writers used and reading the prophetic-and-narrative substance more fully because of the attention.

The deeper substance is the OT theology of standardized measurement as the infrastructure of just commerce, accurate prophetic warning, and precise sacrificial obedience. The homer’s large-unit reckoning was no less precision-bound than the gerah’s small-unit weight; the LORD’s holiness extended to both ends of the measurement scale, requiring just balances and accurate measures throughout. The contemporary application of this measurement-theology is broader than weights-and-measures-ethics narrowly considered: it teaches that God’s holiness extends to the precision of every transaction, every promise, every commitment, every account. The saint’s integrity is to be precision-shaped, not approximation-shaped. The homer-precision of OT agricultural reckoning has its New Covenant analog in the saint’s commitment to precise honesty in every dimension of his stewardship and witness—a precision that mirrors the God who measured both gerahs and homers with equal exactness.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chōmer (a heap, large quantity), from chāmar (to heap); the largest Hebrew dry measure (10 ephahs); used across OT for substantial agricultural reckoning, prophetic crop-warnings, divine provision/judgment narratives, and the standardized measurements of the Levitical and prophetic literature.

expand to see more

Hebrew chōmer (H2563) — homer, a heap; the largest Hebrew dry-measure (Num 11:32; Lev 27:16; Isa 5:10; Ezek 45:11, 14; Hos 3:2).

Hebrew kōr (H3734) — kor (also the largest dry measure, equivalent to the homer; 1 Kgs 4:22).

Hebrew ’ēphāh (H374) — ephah (one-tenth of a homer).

Hebrew ‘ōmer (H6016) — omer (one-tenth of an ephah; daily manna ration in Ex 16:36).
